patient_information: A 55-year-old, previously healthy Swiss couple, both fitness instructors. No other comorbidities or relevant medical history is mentioned.
chief_complaint: A 55-year-old man presented with fever, myalgias, and generalized weakness for 4 days, followed by shortness of breath. His wife presented three weeks later with similar complaints.
history_of_present_illness: The husband developed a fever of 39°C, myalgias, and generalized weakness on his flight back to Switzerland, which did not respond to symptomatic treatment. Four days later at the hospital, he remained febrile and was too weak to walk unassisted. He then developed shortness of breath with oxygen desaturation. His wife presented three weeks later with similar complaints and deteriorated rapidly over 24 hours after admission, developing cardiorespiratory failure and multi-organ failure.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The couple had recently returned from a 3-month trip from Ecuador to Chile. The last month of their trip was spent hiking, camping, and taking occasional mud baths in the Chile-Argentinian border region. The mode of transmission remained unclear; both human-to-human-transmission and acquisition from a common source were considered possible.
vitals: Husband at presentation: Blood pressure 90/55 mmHg, pulse 120 beats per minute, oxygen saturation 94% on ambient air, and temperature 39°C (102.2°F). Wife on admission: normal blood pressure, heart rate and oxygen saturation, temperature 38.6°C (101.5°F).
physical_exam: For both the husband and wife, there were no abnormal findings on cardiopulmonary auscultation at the time of their respective admissions.
labs_and_diagnostics: On admission, the husband's labs showed WCC 7.3 G/L with 35% band neutrophils, platelets 48 G/L, and CRP 68 mg/L. His wife's labs showed WCC 1.88 G/L, platelets 98 G/L, and CRP 7 mg/L. Both had normal glomerular filtration rates and transaminases. The husband's respiratory pathogen panel and HIV test were negative. Chest radiography was normal at presentation in both patients, but during the course of the disease, both developed extensive bilateral infiltrates with pleural effusions.
differential_diagnosis: The differential diagnosis for acute respiratory distress syndrome after travel to South America included influenza and other respiratory viruses, pneumococcal pneumonia, and severe malaria. Rickettsial diseases like spotted fever group rickettsiosis and scrub typhus were considered. New World hantaviruses were a strong consideration due to the cardiopulmonary presentation, the long incubation period which could explain the three-week gap between cases, and the potential for human-to-human transmission.
management_and_clinical_course: The husband was transferred to the ICU for non-invasive ventilator support for 5 days and made a full recovery after a month of rehabilitation. His wife experienced a more dramatic course, requiring extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) for nearly a month. She developed multi-organ failure with renal replacement therapy and disseminated intravascular coagulation, leading to profuse bleeding and requiring mass transfusions. She underwent several surgical interventions for bleeding complications, developed nosocomial infections, and remained in intensive care for 5 months, followed by an additional 12 months in rehabilitation.
final_diagnosis: Both patients were diagnosed with Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS) caused by Andesvirus (ANDV), a New World species of the family Hantaviridae. The diagnosis was confirmed by both PCR and serology. This diagnosis explained the severe cardiorespiratory failure, thrombocytopenia, and the epidemiological link to their travel in a region where ANDV is endemic.
